<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Several nations are considered foreign adversaries by hawkish policymakers. These countries often include Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela. Most foreign adversaries are pariah states, either for their military aggression against neighbors or totalitarian dictatorships.
But one--the People's Republic of China--seeks to expand its global influence, entangling it into a growing economic, diplomatic, and military rivalry with the U.S. that foreign policy scholars label ``Thucydides's Trap.'' In this phenomenon, the rise of one power threatens a more established power, leading to competition, and potentially conflict, between them. Additionally, the Communist Party's tight control of the P.R.C. government and its nominal ideology drive fundamental differences between the political economies of the P.R.C. and the U.S. While the Party therefore has coercive influence over the decisions and activities of citizens and businesses, private property and markets exist in the P.R.C., complicating descriptions of it and the Party as strictly socialist entities.
Party-controlled firms, and companies affiliated with other foreign adversaries, sometimes employ business and competitive practices that are underhanded, illegal, and immoral. These tactics include intellectual property (IP) theft, counterfeit goods, predatory investment, and slavery.
When companies--especially in the P.R.C.--do not employ these practices, however, U.S. businesses of all sizes benefit tremendously from trade and collaboration. The P.R.C. has the world's second-largest economy after the U.S., with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of almost $19.4 trillion, and has been a top U.S. trading partner since its accession to the World Trade Organization in 2001.\1\ Small businesses reap lower costs, greater innovation, and access to vast sales markets, from their trade and collaboration with P.R.C. partners--in areas outside of critical and military technology. Furthermore, the U.S. has attracted scores of P.R.C. scientists and engineers, leveraging their skills and expertise to serve U.S. national interests, instead of our competitor's. This net outflow of talent has created and reinforced a ``brain drain'' from top P.R.C. labs and companies.
\1\Karen M. Sutter, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF11284, U.S.-China Trade Relations (Sep. 9, 2025).
On March 25, 2026, the full Committee held a hearing titled ``Defending Main Street: Combating CCP Threats to America's Small Businesses,'' at which Dr. Rush Doshi, the C.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, testified to the P.R.C.'s strategic ambitions and capacity to compete with the U.S., emphasizing that the key to successfully outcompeting the P.R.C. lies in greater volumes and coordination of domestic and allied scientific research, manufacturing, and capital access--not President Trump's tariffs, One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or racism. As part of its oversight duties, the Committee will closely monitor the implementation of this legislation, if enacted into law, to ensure that it is laser-focused on foreign conduct harming small businesses, and not on ethnicity or national origin.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
